s: Men are included among all people for whom prayer is to be made, and God desires their salvation. The author wants men in every place to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting. Christ Jesus is the mediator between God and men.

Women are told to adorn themselves in decent clothing with modesty and propriety, and with good works fitting for those professing godliness. They are to learn in quietness with full submission. The text says the woman will be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love, and holiness with sobriety.

l: prayer for all people, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: The author exhorts first of all that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men, including kings and those in high places. The stated purpose is that believers may lead a tranquil and quiet life in godliness and reverence, and it is called good and acceptable to God.

God desires all people to be saved and to come to full knowledge of the truth. Christ Jesus gave himself as a ransom for all. The text also says the woman will be saved through her childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness with sobriety.

l: women's adornment and conduct, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: Women are to dress decently with modesty and propriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or expensive clothing. Their adornment is to be good works, appropriate for women professing godliness. They are also to learn in quietness with full submission.

l: women's teaching and authority restriction, 1 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: The author says he does not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but that she be in quietness. He gives as reasons that Adam was formed first, then Eve, and that Adam wasn't deceived while the woman was and fell into disobedience.

Chapter 3 sets out the qualifications for two groups of church leaders: the overseer and the servants. The overseer must be without reproach, faithful to one wife, self-controlled, a good teacher, gentle, not greedy, and one who rules his own household well; he must not be a new convert and must have a good reputation among outsiders. Servants must likewise be reverent, honest, not addicted to wine or greedy for money, hold the faith with a pure conscience, and be tested first, and their wives must also be reverent and faithful. The writer says he hopes to come soon, but is writing so the reader will know how people ought to behave in God's house, which is the assembly of the living God. The chapter closes by declaring the mystery of godliness great: God was revealed in the flesh and received up in glory.

The overseer is described as someone who desires a good work. He must be without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, and good at teaching, and not a drinker, violent, quarrelsome, or greedy. He must rule his own house well with obedient children, since failing at that would make him unfit to care for God's assembly. He must not be a new convert, lest he be puffed up and fall into the devil's condemnation, and he must have good testimony from outsiders to avoid reproach and the devil's snare.

Servants must be reverent, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money, and must hold the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. They are to be tested first and serve only if blameless. Their wives must be reverent, not slanderers, temperate, and faithful in all things. Servants must be husbands of one wife and rule their children and houses well, and those who serve well gain a good standing and great boldness in the faith in Christ Jesus.

God is called the living God, whose house is the assembly. In the closing statement, God is said to have been revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.

God's assembly is identified as God's house and as the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. The writer explains that his instructions exist so the reader will know how people ought to behave in it. The overseer is charged with taking care of it, and his ability to do so is tied to how well he rules his own house.

The mystery of godliness is declared, without controversy, to be great. It is described as God being revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.

The chapter opens with the Spirit's warning that in later times some will fall away from the faith, following seducing spirits and doctrines of demons spread by hypocritical liars who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods. The writer counters that everything God created is good and sanctified by God's word and prayer when received with thanksgiving. He then urges the addressee to instruct the brothers, refuse profane fables, and exercise himself toward godliness, which holds promise for this life and the next. The addressee is told to be an example to believers despite his youth, to attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching, and not to neglect the gift given him by prophecy and the laying on of the elders' hands. The chapter closes by urging him to watch himself and his teaching, since doing so will save both himself and his hearers.
The Spirit speaks expressly, warning that in later times some will fall away from the faith. This is the source of the prophetic warning that opens the chapter.

God is said to have created foods to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. Every creature of God is good, and it is sanctified through his word. He is the living God, in whom the writer and his companions trust, and the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe.

l: those who fall away from the faith, 1 Timothy, Chapter 4
s: In later times some will fall away, paying attention to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons. They are led by hypocritical men who speak lies, are branded in their own conscience as with a hot iron, forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods.

Foods are described as created by God to be received with thanksgiving by believers. Nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving, because it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.

Believers are those who know the truth and receive God's creation with thanksgiving. The addressee is told to be an example to them in word, way of life, love, spirit, faith, and purity. God is the Savior of all men, especially of them.

The addressee is told to instruct the brothers, refuse profane and old wives' fables, exercise himself toward godliness, and let no one despise his youth. He is to devote himself to reading, exhortation, and teaching until the writer comes, not neglect his gift given by prophecy with the laying on of the elders' hands, and keep watch over himself. By continuing in these things he will save himself and those who hear him.

Godliness is something to exercise oneself toward. It is contrasted with bodily exercise, which has some value, while godliness has value in all things and holds the promise of the life now and of that to come.

The addressee is told to command and teach these things and to attend to teaching until the writer comes. He is to pay attention to his teaching and continue in it, for doing so will save both himself and his hearers. The good doctrine is also what has nourished him.

Chapter 5 gives instructions on how to treat different groups within the community. It opens with how to address older and younger men and women, then spends most of its length on widows: who counts as a widow indeed, who should be enrolled (over sixty, wife of one man, known for good works), why younger widows should be refused enrollment and encouraged to marry, and the duty of families to support their own widows so the assembly is not burdened. It then turns to elders, who are to be counted worthy of double honor, protected from accusations without two or three witnesses, and publicly reproved if they sin. The chapter closes with commands to act without prejudice, not to lay hands hastily on anyone, to keep oneself pure, to use a little wine for the stomach and frequent infirmities, and a note that sins and good works eventually become evident.

Widows indeed are to be honored. A true widow is desolate, sets her hope on God, and continues in petitions and prayers night and day. To be enrolled she must be at least sixty, have been the wife of one man, and be approved for good works such as raising children, showing hospitality, washing the saints' feet, relieving the afflicted, and following every good work. The assembly is to relieve them once families have done their part.

Younger widows are to be refused enrollment, because they may grow wanton against Christ and desire to marry, incurring condemnation for rejecting their first pledge. They are said to learn idleness, going from house to house as gossips and busybodies, and some have already turned away after Satan. The text desires that they marry, bear children, and rule the household, giving the adversary no occasion for insult.

Elders who rule well are to be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching, supported by the sayings about not muzzling the ox and the laborer deserving wages. An accusation against an elder may be received only on the word of two or three witnesses. Those who sin are to be reproved in the sight of all so that the rest may fear.

l: children and grandchildren (of widows), 1 Timothy, Chapter 5
s: Children and grandchildren of a widow are told to learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents. This is described as acceptable in the sight of God.

Any believing man or woman who has widows in the family is told to relieve them. This keeps the assembly from being burdened so that it can relieve those who are widows indeed. Anyone who does not provide for his own, especially his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

God is the one in whose sight care for family is acceptable, and the true widow sets her hope on him. The writer's charge about impartiality is given in the sight of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels.

l: care for widows and family obligations, 1 Timothy, Chapter 5
s: Responsibility for widows falls first on their own children, grandchildren, and believing relatives, and failure to provide for one's household is called a denial of the faith. Only widows indeed, meeting the stated criteria, are supported by the assembly, and younger widows are directed toward marriage and household life instead. The aim is that the assembly not be burdened and that none be without reproach.

l: honor and discipline of elders, 1 Timothy, Chapter 5
s: Elders who rule well receive double honor and wages, especially those who teach, and are shielded by the two-or-three-witness rule for accusations. Persistent sin is reproved publicly, and the instruction is to be carried out without prejudice or partiality. Hands are not to be laid hastily on anyone, and the text notes that some sins and good works are evident at once while others emerge later.

Chapter 6 gives instructions to Timothy about how different groups should live and what he must guard. Bondservants are told to honor their masters, including believing masters, so that God's name and the doctrine are not blasphemed. Those who teach a different doctrine, being conceited and quarrelsome and treating godliness as a means of gain, are to be avoided, while godliness with contentment is called great gain and the love of money is named a root of all kinds of evil. Timothy is told to flee these things, pursue righteousness and the other virtues, fight the good fight, and keep the commandment blameless until the appearing of Jesus Christ, whom God will show at the right time. Rich people are to be charged not to be arrogant or trust in riches but to hope in God, do good, and share, and Timothy is finally told to guard what was entrusted to him and avoid empty chatter and falsely called knowledge.

Timothy is addressed as a man of God and told to flee the love of money and follow righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. He is commanded to fight the good fight of faith, take hold of eternal life, keep the commandment blameless, charge the rich, and guard what was committed to him. He is also told to withdraw from false teachers and turn away from empty chatter and falsely called knowledge.

Jesus Christ is named as the source of the sound words to which true doctrine is tied. He testified the good confession before Pontius Pilate, and his appearing is the point until which the commandment is to be kept blameless. At the right time he will be shown as the blessed and only Ruler, King of kings and Lord of lords.

God gives life to all things and is the one before whom Timothy is commanded. He alone has immortality, dwells in unapproachable light, and is unseen by any man. He richly provides everything to enjoy, and the rich are told to set their hope on him rather than on riches.

Bondservants under the yoke are told to count their masters worthy of all honor so that God's name and the doctrine are not blasphemed. Those with believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers, but serve them all the more.
Masters are to be honored by their bondservants. Believing masters are described as brothers who are believing and beloved and who partake of the benefit of the service.

Those who teach a different doctrine and do not consent to sound words are called conceited and knowing nothing. They are obsessed with disputes and word battles that produce envy, strife, insults, and evil suspicions, and they suppose godliness is a means of gain. Timothy is told to withdraw from them, and some who professed falsely called knowledge have wandered from the faith.

Those who are rich in the present age are to be charged not to be arrogant or set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God. They are to do good, be rich in good works, and be ready to share. In doing so they lay up a good foundation for the time to come and lay hold of eternal life.

Godliness with contentment is declared to be great gain, in contrast to those who treat godliness as a means of gain. Contentment is illustrated by being satisfied with food and clothing, since nothing was brought into the world and nothing can be carried out.

The love of money is called a root of all kinds of evil. Those determined to be rich fall into temptation, a snare, and foolish and harmful lusts that drown people in ruin and destruction. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed and pierced themselves with many sorrows.

Sound doctrine is described as the words of the Lord Jesus Christ and the doctrine according to godliness. Misbehavior by bondservants risks causing it to be blasphemed, and those who do not consent to it are labeled conceited teachers of a different doctrine. Timothy is told to teach and exhort these things and to guard what was committed to him.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will, greets Timothy, his beloved child, and says he thanks God and remembers Timothy's tears and the sincere faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. He urges Timothy to stir up the gift of God received through the laying on of Paul's hands, reminding him that God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control rather than fear. Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of Paul as prisoner, because God saved and called people according to his own purpose and grace, revealed through Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the Good News. Paul says he was appointed preacher, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles, suffers for this, yet is not ashamed, and charges Timothy to hold sound words and guard the good thing committed to him through the Holy Spirit. He notes that all in Asia, including Phygelus and Hermogenes, turned away from him, while he asks mercy for the house of Onesiphorus, who refreshed him, was not ashamed of his chain, and sought him out in Rome.

Paul writes as an apostle of Jesus Christ by God's will and was appointed a preacher, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles. He thanks God, longs to see Timothy, suffers yet is not ashamed because he is persuaded God can guard what he has committed to him, and notes that all in Asia turned away from him.

Timothy is addressed as Paul's beloved child, remembered for his tears and for sincere faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. He is urged to stir up God's gift, not be ashamed of the testimony or of Paul, endure hardship for the Good News, hold sound words, and guard the good thing committed to him through the Holy Spirit.

God is served by Paul with a pure conscience and gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control rather than fear. He saved and called people with a holy calling according to his own purpose and grace, and is able to guard what Paul has committed to him until that day.

Christ Jesus is the one in whom the promise of life lies and from whom, with God the Father, grace, mercy, and peace come. As Savior he appeared, abolished death, and brought life and immortality to light through the Good News; grace was given in him before times eternal.

Paul asks the Lord to grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed Paul and was not ashamed of his chain. When in Rome he diligently sought Paul and found him, and Paul prays he will find the Lord's mercy in that day, noting Timothy knows well his service at Ephesus.

The Good News is what Timothy is told to endure hardship for, according to God's power. Through it life and immortality were brought to light, and Paul was appointed as its preacher, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles.

l: gift of God (Timothy's gift), 2 Timothy, 2 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: The gift of God is in Timothy through the laying on of Paul's hands, and Paul reminds him to stir it up. It is linked to the spirit God gave, one of power, love, and self-control rather than fear.

l: Paul's suffering and imprisonment, 2 Timothy, 2 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: Paul is a prisoner, with a chain of which Onesiphorus was not ashamed, and he suffers because of his appointment as preacher, apostle, and teacher. He says he is not ashamed, and he calls Timothy to share in enduring hardship for the Good News.

l: salvation and holy calling, 2 Timothy, 2 Timothy / Chapter 1
s: God saved and called people with a holy calling, not according to their works but according to his own purpose and grace given in Christ Jesus before times eternal. This has now been revealed through the appearing of the Savior, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light.

The speaker urges his child, the addressee, to be strengthened in Christ's grace, to pass on what he has heard to faithful men who can teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, athlete, and farmer. He tells him to remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, and says he himself suffers to the point of chains, though God's word isn't chained, and endures all things for the chosen ones. He quotes a trustworthy saying about dying, living, enduring, and reigning with Christ, and about Christ remaining faithful even when people are faithless. He warns against arguing about words and empty chatter, naming Hymenaeus and Philetus as men who say the resurrection is already past and overthrow some people's faith. He contrasts vessels of honor and dishonor in a large house, tells the addressee to flee youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, and describes the Lord's servant as gentle and patient in correcting opponents, in hope that God may grant them repentance.

Jesus Christ is presented as the source of grace in which the addressee is to be strengthened, and the one to be remembered as risen from the dead and of the offspring of David. He is the one with whom believers die, live, and reign, and he remains faithful even when people are faithless, for he can't deny himself.

God's word is said not to be chained, even though the speaker is imprisoned. God's firm foundation stands with the seal that the Lord knows those who are his, and God may give opponents repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth. The addressee is to present himself approved by God.

The addressee is told to be strengthened in grace, to commit what he has heard to faithful men who can teach others, and to endure hardship as a good soldier. He is also told to remind others not to argue about words, to present himself approved as a workman who handles the Word of Truth properly, to shun empty chatter and youthful lusts, and to pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace.

The speaker addresses his child with instruction and describes his own suffering to the point of chains as a criminal for the Good News. He says he endures all things for the chosen ones' sake so that they may obtain salvation in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.

The Lord's servant is described as one who must not quarrel but be gentle toward all, able to teach, and patient. He corrects those who oppose him in gentleness, in the hope that God may give them repentance and that they may recover from the devil's snare.

l: false teachers' empty chatter, 2 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: Empty chatter is to be shunned because it goes further in ungodliness and consumes like gangrene. Hymenaeus and Philetus are named as examples, having erred about the truth by saying the resurrection is already past and overthrowing the faith of some.

l: the Word of Truth, 2 Timothy, Chapter 2
s: The addressee is told to handle the Word of Truth properly, as a workman who doesn't need to be ashamed. Those who err concerning the truth, like Hymenaeus and Philetus, are contrasted with this, and opponents may come to a full knowledge of the truth.

Enduring hardship is urged on the addressee through the images of a good soldier, an athlete competing by the rules, and a laboring farmer. The speaker models it by enduring all things for the chosen ones, and the saying promises that those who endure will also reign with Christ.

A large house is used as an image containing not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor. It illustrates that a person who purges himself can become suitable for the master's use.

Vessels in the large house are of gold, silver, wood, and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor. Anyone who purges himself from these will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, suitable for the master's use, and prepared for every good work.

The chapter warns that in the last days grievous times will come, when men will be lovers of self, money, and pleasure, holding a form of godliness while denying its power. The speaker tells the addressee to turn away from such people, who creep into houses and captivate gullible women, and who oppose the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. The speaker says their folly will become evident and they will go no further, though evil men and impostors will grow worse, deceiving and being deceived. The addressee is contrasted as one who followed the speaker's teaching, conduct, and sufferings, including persecutions at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra from which the Lord delivered the speaker. The addressee is urged to remain in what was learned, grounded in the holy Scriptures known since infancy, which are God-breathed and equip people for every good work.

l: men of the last days (the corrupt men), 2 Timothy, Chapter 3
s: They are described as lovers of self, money, and pleasure rather than God, boastful, arrogant, disobedient, unforgiving, and holding a form of godliness while denying its power. Some creep into houses and captivate gullible women, are always learning but never reach the truth, and oppose the truth like Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. They will go no further, as their folly will be evident to all, yet evil men and impostors will grow worse, deceiving and being deceived.
They are announced as a time when grievous times will come. The period is marked by the rise of men with a long list of vices, including a form of godliness without its power.

The holy Scriptures, known to the addressee from infancy, are able to make one wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. Every Scripture is said to be God-breathed and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness, so that each person who belongs to God may be complete and thoroughly equipped for every good work.

The speaker recounts persecutions and sufferings at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, which he endured and from which the Lord delivered him. It is stated that all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.

The speaker instructs the addressee to turn away from the corrupt men and recalls his own teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, and steadfastness. He endured persecutions at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and says the Lord delivered him out of them all.

The addressee is told to turn away from the corrupt men and is commended as one who followed the speaker's teaching, conduct, and endurance. He is urged to remain in what he has learned and been assured of, knowing from whom he learned it, and is reminded that he has known the holy Scriptures from infancy.

Paul solemnly charges Timothy before God and Christ to preach the word with patience, warning that people will come to reject sound doctrine for teachers who please their itching ears and for fables. Paul says his death is near, declaring that he has fought the good fight, finished the course and kept the faith, and that a crown of righteousness awaits him and all who love Christ's appearing. He asks Timothy to come soon, bringing Mark, the cloak left with Carpus at Troas, and the books and parchments, since Demas has deserted him, others have gone elsewhere, and only Luke remains. Paul warns of Alexander the coppersmith, recalls that no one stood with him at his first defense while the Lord strengthened and delivered him, and closes with greetings to Prisca, Aquila and the house of Onesiphorus, news of Erastus and Trophimus, and greetings from Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia and the brothers.

Paul charges Timothy to preach the word and declares that his own departure has come, saying he has fought the good fight, finished the course and kept the faith. He asks Timothy to come before winter and bring Mark, his cloak and the books, reports that Demas and others have left him and that only Luke is with him, and says the Lord stood by him and delivered him at his first defense.

Timothy is solemnly charged to preach the word urgently, reprove, rebuke and exhort with patience, stay sober, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist and fulfill his ministry. He is asked to come to Paul soon, before winter, bringing Mark, the cloak from Carpus at Troas and the books, and to beware of Alexander the coppersmith.

Jesus Christ is named as the one before whom Paul gives his charge, who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his Kingdom. The Lord is said to stand by and strengthen Paul, to deliver him from every evil work, to preserve him for his heavenly Kingdom, and to give the crown of righteousness as righteous judge.

l: those who will not listen to sound doctrine, 2 Timothy, Chapter 4
s: Paul predicts a time when people will not listen to sound doctrine but, having itching ears, will heap up teachers according to their own lusts. They will turn their ears from the truth and turn to fables.

Paul commands Timothy to preach the word, being urgent in season and out of season, reproving, rebuking and exhorting with all patience and teaching. It is tied to doing the work of an evangelist, and Paul recounts that through him the message was fully proclaimed so that all the Gentiles might hear.

Paul says he is already being offered and the time of his departure has come. He views it with confidence, having fought the good fight, finished the course and kept the faith, and expects the Lord to preserve him for his heavenly Kingdom.
Paul says the crown of righteousness is stored up for him, to be given by the Lord, the righteous judge, on that day. It is promised not to Paul only but to all who have loved Christ's appearing.

l: Titus, Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: Paul, a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to Titus, whom he calls his true child in a common faith, greeting him with grace, mercy, and peace and recalling God's promise of eternal life. Paul explains that he left Titus in Crete to set in order what was lacking and to appoint elders in every city. He lists the qualifications for these elders, or overseers: blameless, the husband of one wife, with believing children, hospitable, self-controlled, and holding to the faithful word so as to exhort in sound doctrine and convict those who contradict. He warns of many unruly men, vain talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, who overthrow whole houses for dishonest gain and must be silenced. Quoting one of their own prophets, who called Cretans liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons, Paul tells Titus to reprove them sharply so they may be sound in the faith, and he describes the defiled as professing God while denying him by their deeds.

l: Paul, Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: Paul identifies himself as a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, entrusted with God's message according to the commandment of God our Savior. He writes to Titus, reminding him that he left him in Crete to set things in order and appoint elders as Paul directed. He also instructs Titus to stop the mouths of unruly deceivers and to reprove the Cretans sharply.

l: Titus, Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: Titus is addressed by Paul as his true child according to a common faith and is greeted with grace, mercy, and peace. He was left in Crete to set in order the things that were lacking and to appoint elders in every city. He is told to reprove the Cretans sharply so that they may be sound in the faith.

l: God, Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: God is described as one who cannot lie and who promised eternal life before time began. In his own time he revealed his word through the message entrusted to Paul, and he is called Savior. Overseers are described as his stewards, and those who are defiled profess to know him but deny him by their deeds.

l: Crete, Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: Crete is the place where Paul left Titus so that he could set in order the things that were lacking. Elders are to be appointed in every city there. It is also where many unruly men, vain talkers and deceivers, are active.

l: Cretans, Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: Cretans are characterized by one of their own prophets as always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons, and Paul says this testimony is true. Titus is told to reprove them sharply so that they may be sound in the faith and not pay attention to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn from the truth.

l: elders (appointed in every city of Crete), Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: Elders are to be appointed by Titus in every city, following Paul's direction. They must be blameless, the husband of one wife, with believing children not accused of loose or unruly behavior. As overseers and God's stewards, they must not be self-pleasing, easily angered, given to wine, violent, or greedy, but hospitable, lovers of good, sober minded, fair, holy, and self-controlled, holding to the faithful word so as to exhort in sound doctrine and convict those who contradict.

l: unruly men (deceivers in Crete), Titus, Letter to Titus / Chapter 1
s: Unruly men are described as many in number, vain talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision. Their mouths must be stopped because they overthrow whole houses, teaching what they ought not for dishonest gain. They profess to know God but deny him by their deeds, and are called abominable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work.

Chapter 2 instructs the addressee to speak what fits sound doctrine and to teach each group in the community. Older men are to be temperate, sensible, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. Older women are to be reverent and good teachers who train young wives to love their husbands and children and to be chaste, kind, and workers at home. Younger men are to be sober minded, and servants are to be subject to their masters, honest, and faithful. The addressee must be an example of good works with sound speech, and the chapter grounds this conduct in the grace of God, which brings salvation, teaches godly living, and looks for the appearing of God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem and purify a people zealous for good works.

God is called our Savior, and his word is not to be blasphemed through the conduct of believers. His grace has appeared bringing salvation to all men, and he is described as great, with a glory that is awaited.

Jesus Christ is called our great God and Savior, whose glorious appearing is the blessed hope believers look for. He gave himself for us to redeem us from all iniquity and to purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.
Older men are to be temperate, sensible, and sober minded. They are also to be sound in faith, in love, and in perseverance.
Older women are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers, and not enslaved to much wine. They are to be teachers of what is good, training the young wives.

Young wives are to be trained by the older women to love their husbands and children. They are to be sober minded, chaste, workers at home, kind, and in subjection to their own husbands, so that God's word is not blasphemed.
Younger men are to be exhorted to be sober minded.

Servants are to be exhorted to be in subjection to their own masters, well-pleasing in all things, not contradicting or stealing. By showing all good fidelity they adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things.

l: addressee (the one instructed to speak and exhort), Titus, Chapter 2
s: The addressee is told to say what fits sound doctrine and to exhort the younger men and servants. He is to be an example of good works, showing integrity, seriousness, incorruptibility, and unconditionable speech, so that any opponent is ashamed. He is to speak, exhort, and reprove with all authority and let no one despise him.
Sound doctrine is what the addressee is to speak about, with teaching fitted to each group. The doctrine of God our Savior is adorned by the good fidelity of servants.

The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men. It instructs believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age while looking for the blessed hope.

Chapter 3 instructs the readers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be gentle and humble toward all, and to be ready for every good work. It recalls that the believers were once foolish, disobedient and hateful, but that God our Savior, through his kindness and mercy and not their works, saved them by the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior, making them heirs of eternal life. The writer urges that believers be careful to maintain good works, shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife and disputes about the law, and avoid a factious man after two warnings. He closes with instructions to come to him at Nicopolis when Artemas or Tychicus is sent, to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, and with greetings and a blessing of grace.

God our Savior is said to have shown his kindness and love toward mankind. Not because of any works of righteousness but according to his mercy, he saved the believers through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit, and he justified them by his grace so that they might be heirs of eternal life.
Jesus Christ our Savior is named as the one through whom God richly poured out the Holy Spirit on the believers. He is also called Savior in this unit.

The believers are told to be subject to rulers and authorities, obedient, gentle, humble toward all, and ready for every good work. They are reminded that they were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, and hateful, but were saved by God's mercy and made heirs of eternal life. They are told to shun foolish disputes, avoid a factious man after two warnings, and learn to maintain good works to meet necessary needs so they are not unfruitful. They send greetings and receive a blessing of grace.

Good works are not the basis of salvation, since God saved the believers not by works of righteousness that they did. Yet believers are to be ready for every good work, to be careful to maintain them, and to practice them to meet necessary needs so they are not unfruitful. The text calls these things good and profitable to men.

Salvation is described as coming from God's kindness, love and mercy rather than human works. It occurs through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. Being justified by grace, believers become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

Foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law are to be shunned because they are unprofitable and vain. A factious man who persists after a first and second warning is to be avoided, as he is perverted, sinful, and self-condemned.

Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to chosen ones living as foreigners in the Dispersion across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. He blesses God the Father of Jesus Christ for causing believers to be born again to a living hope and an inheritance reserved in Heaven, and for guarding them through faith for a coming salvation. He says their trials test their faith like gold in fire, and that the prophets and angels longed to understand this salvation. He then urges the readers to prepare their minds, to be holy as God is holy, and to live in reverent fear, since they were redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, the lamb without blemish. He closes by calling them to love one another fervently, having been born again through the enduring word of God, which is the Good News preached to them.

Peter identifies himself as an apostle of Jesus Christ and writes to the chosen ones living as foreigners in the Dispersion. He blesses God, encourages the readers in their trials, and exhorts them to holiness, reverent fear, and fervent love for one another.

Jesus Christ is the one whose resurrection from the dead gives believers a living hope, and whose blood sprinkles and redeems them as a lamb without blemish or spot. He was foreknown before the foundation of the world and revealed in this last age, and God raised him from the dead and gave him glory. His sufferings and the glories that would follow were predicted by the Spirit of Christ in the prophets, and his revelation is when believers' faith will result in praise, glory, and honor.

God the Father is the God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, and according to his great mercy he caused believers to be born again to a living hope. His foreknowledge is the basis of the readers' election, and his power guards them through faith for salvation. He is holy, calls his people to be holy, judges without respect of persons according to each one's work, and raised Christ from the dead and gave him glory.

l: chosen ones (recipients of the letter), 1 Peter, 1 Peter / Chapter 1
s: The chosen ones are foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. They rejoice though grieved in various trials, love Jesus Christ without having seen him, and are guarded by God's power through faith. They are told to prepare their minds, be sober, be holy in all their behavior, live in reverent fear, and love one another fervently from the heart, having purified their souls in obedience to the truth.

Salvation is ready to be revealed in the last time, and believers receive it as the result of their faith, the salvation of their souls. The prophets sought and searched diligently concerning it and prophesied of the grace that would come to the readers, and angels desire to look into it. It involves redemption from the useless way of life handed down from their fathers, by the precious blood of Christ.

l: new birth / living hope, 1 Peter, 1 Peter / Chapter 1
s: God, according to his great mercy, caused believers to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. This leads to an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance that doesn't fade away, reserved in Heaven. The new birth is of incorruptible seed, through the word of God, which lives and remains forever.

Believers are commanded to be holy in all their behavior, just as God who called them is holy, citing the scripture "You shall be holy, for I am holy." This calls for obedience as children of obedience, not conforming to their former lusts formed in ignorance. It is paired with reverent fear during their time as foreigners, and with sincere, fervent love for one another.

The Good News was preached to the readers by the Holy Spirit sent out from heaven, announcing the things the prophets served by foretelling. It is identified with the word of the Lord that endures forever, in contrast to grass that withers and flowers that fall. Angels desire to look into these things.

Chapter 2 urges believers to put away wickedness, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and evil speaking, and to long for pure spiritual milk in order to grow. It describes Jesus Christ as a living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious to God, and as the chief cornerstone, with believers built up as a spiritual house and holy priesthood, while the disobedient stumble over him. Believers are called a chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation and God's people, who now have mercy and are to live as foreigners and pilgrims with good behavior among the nations. They are told to submit to the king, governors and masters, to honor all, love the brotherhood and fear God, living as free people who are bondservants of God. The chapter ends with Christ's example of suffering unjustly without sin or retaliation, bearing sins on the tree so that believers might live to righteousness and return to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

Jesus Christ is described as a living stone, rejected by men but chosen by God and precious, and as the chief cornerstone in whom believers will not be disappointed. He suffered for believers, leaving an example: he did not sin, no deceit was found in his mouth, he did not curse or threaten when abused, and he committed himself to the one who judges righteously. He bore the sins of believers in his body on the tree, so that they might die to sins and live to righteousness, and his wounds healed them; he is called the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

God chose the living stone and made it precious, and he is the one to whom believers' spiritual sacrifices are acceptable through Jesus Christ. He called believers out of darkness into his marvelous light, made them his own people, and showed them mercy. His will is that believers put foolish men to silence by doing well, he is to be feared, and he judges righteously.

l: chosen ones (recipients of the letter), 1 Peter, Chapter 2
s: Believers are told to put away wickedness, deceit, hypocrisies, envies and evil speaking and to long for spiritual milk so they may grow. They are built up as living stones into a spiritual house and holy priesthood, and are called a chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation and people for God's possession who have now obtained mercy. As foreigners and pilgrims they are to abstain from fleshly lusts, keep good behavior among the nations, and live as free people who are God's bondservants, having returned to the Shepherd after going astray like sheep.

l: suffering for doing good, 1 Peter, Chapter 2
s: Enduring pain and suffering unjustly because of conscience toward God is called commendable, whereas patiently enduring a beating for one's own sin earns no glory. Patiently enduring suffering while doing well is commendable with God. Believers were called to this, following the example of Christ, who suffered for them without sinning or retaliating.

Believers are told to subject themselves to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake, whether to the king as supreme or to governors sent to punish evildoers and praise those who do well. This is God's will, since by well-doing they put to silence the ignorance of foolish men, and their freedom must not be used as a cloak for wickedness. Servants are told to submit to their masters with all respect, including the wicked ones, and all are to honor all men and the king.

Chapter 3 first instructs wives to be in subjection to their husbands so that disobedient husbands may be won by their behavior, urging inner adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit over outward adornment, with Sarah and Abraham as the example. Husbands are told to live with their wives according to knowledge, honoring them as the weaker vessel and as joint heirs of the grace of life, so that their prayers are not hindered. All the addressees are then urged to be like-minded, loving, and to bless rather than return evil, citing a quotation about seeking peace and about the Lord's eyes being on the righteous. The chapter says that suffering for righteousness is a blessing, that believers should be ready to answer for their hope with humility and a good conscience, and that it is better to suffer for doing right than for doing evil. It closes with Christ, who suffered once for sins, was made alive in the Spirit, preached to the spirits in prison from the days of Noah, and is now at God's right hand with angels, authorities and powers subject to him, while baptism is described as a symbol that saves through his resurrection.

Wives are told to be in subjection to their own husbands so that husbands who do not obey the Word may be won without a word by their pure behavior. Their beauty is to come from the hidden person of the heart, a gentle and quiet spirit precious to God, as the holy women of the past did, and Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him lord, is the example.

Husbands are told to live with their wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman as the weaker vessel and as a joint heir of the grace of life. The stated reason is that their prayers may not be hindered.

God finds a gentle and quiet spirit very precious, and he waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ship was built. The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears open to their prayer, but his face is against those who do evil. Christ's suffering is said to bring believers to God, and Christ is at God's right hand.

Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring believers to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit. In the Spirit he went and preached to the spirits in prison who were disobedient in Noah's days. Through his resurrection baptism saves, and he is now at God's right hand in heaven with angels, authorities and powers made subject to him.

Suffering for righteousness' sake is declared a blessing, and believers are told not to fear what others fear or be troubled. It is said to be better, if God wills, to suffer for doing right than for doing evil. Christ's own suffering is given as the model, and those who speak against believers as evildoers may be disappointed.

l: chosen ones (recipients of the letter), 1 Peter, Chapter 3
s: Believers are urged to be like-minded, compassionate, loving, tenderhearted and courteous, and not to repay evil for evil or insult for insult but to bless, since they were called to inherit a blessing. They are to sanctify the Lord God in their hearts and always be ready to give an answer about their hope with humility, fear and a good conscience. They are told baptism, a symbol tied to the water of Noah's days, now saves them through Jesus Christ's resurrection.

Chapter 4 urges the addressees to arm themselves with the same mind as Christ, who suffered in the flesh, and to stop living for the lusts of the Gentiles, whose past conduct they describe, in favor of God's will. Those who think it strange that the believers no longer join their excess speak evil of them but will give account to God, who is ready to judge the living and the dead. Because the end of all things is near, the believers are told to be sober, earnest in love, hospitable, and to use their gifts to serve one another so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ. The chapter then tells them not to be astonished at the fiery trial, to rejoice in sharing Christ's sufferings, to avoid suffering as wrongdoers, and not to be ashamed if they suffer as Christians. Judgment begins with the household of God, and those who suffer according to God's will are to entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.

Christ suffered for the believers in the flesh, and his example is the basis for the command to arm themselves with the same mind. Believers share in his sufferings, will rejoice at the revelation of his glory, and glorify God through him; the glory and dominion belong to him forever.

God has a will that believers are to live for, supplies strength for their service, and is glorified in all things through Jesus Christ. He is ready to judge the living and the dead, his household is judged first, and he is described as a faithful Creator to whom those who suffer should entrust their souls.

l: chosen ones (recipients of the letter), 1 Peter, Chapter 4
s: The believers are told to stop living for human lusts and live for God's will, having already spent enough time in the Gentiles' practices. They are commanded to be sober, love earnestly, show hospitality, and serve with their gifts as managers of God's grace. They face a fiery trial and insults for Christ's name, are called blessed, and are told to rejoice, not be ashamed, and entrust their souls to God while doing good.

l: unbelievers (those who think it strange), 1 Peter, Chapter 4
s: They think it strange that the believers no longer run with them into the same excess, and they speak evil of them. They will give account to the one ready to judge the living and the dead, and the text asks what will happen to those who don't obey the Good News of God.

l: suffering for doing good, 1 Peter, Chapter 4
s: Suffering in the flesh is tied to ceasing from sin, and Christ's own suffering is the model. Believers are told not to be astonished at the fiery trial, to rejoice as partakers of Christ's sufferings, and to suffer only as Christians, never as murderers, thieves, evildoers, or meddlers. Those who suffer according to God's will should keep doing good and entrust their souls to him.

Judgment is coming from God, who is ready to judge the living and the dead, and the unbelievers will give account to him. The time has come for it to begin with the household of God, which raises the question of what will happen to the disobedient, the ungodly, and the sinner. The Good News was preached even to the dead so that they might be judged as men in the flesh but live to God in the spirit.

The author, who calls himself a fellow elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings, urges the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and as examples, not for dishonest gain or by lording over others. He tells the younger ones to be subject to the elder and tells everyone to clothe themselves with humility, since God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. The readers are told to cast their worries on God, to be sober and watchful against the devil who prowls like a roaring lion, and to withstand him steadfastly, knowing their brothers elsewhere suffer the same. The author prays that the God of all grace will perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle them after a little suffering. He closes by naming Silvanus as the one through whom he wrote, sending greetings from the woman in Babylon and from Mark, and giving a blessing of peace.

God is described as resisting the proud and giving grace to the humble, and as having a mighty hand under which believers are to humble themselves so that he may exalt them in due time. He cares for his people, called them to his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, and is prayed to as the God of all grace who will perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle them after a little suffering. Glory and power are ascribed to him forever.

Christ Jesus is the one by whom God called believers to his eternal glory. The author calls himself a witness of Christ's sufferings, and the closing blessing offers peace to all who are in Christ Jesus. The text also speaks of the chief Shepherd who will be revealed and bring the crown of glory.

l: elders (the elders among you), 1 Peter, Chapter 5
s: The elders are exhorted to shepherd the flock of God by exercising oversight voluntarily and willingly, not under compulsion or for dishonest gain. They are not to lord it over those entrusted to them but to be examples to the flock. When the chief Shepherd is revealed, they will receive the unfading crown of glory.

The author exhorts the elders as a fellow elder, a witness of Christ's sufferings, and one who will share in the glory to be revealed. He says he wrote briefly through Silvanus, whom he considers a faithful brother, to testify that this is the true grace of God. He sends greetings from the woman in Babylon and from Mark, whom he calls his son, and he closes with a blessing of peace.

The flock of God is the group among the readers that the elders are to shepherd, oversee, and set an example for. The text also addresses the younger ones to be subject to the elder and all to clothe themselves with humility and subject themselves to one another.

The devil is called the readers' adversary and is likened to a roaring lion walking around seeking whom he may devour. Believers are told to be sober, self-controlled, and watchful, and to withstand him steadfast in their faith.

l: suffering for doing good, 1 Peter, Chapter 5
s: Sufferings appear as the author's witnessing of Christ's sufferings and as the same sufferings undergone by the readers' brothers in the world. The readers' own suffering is described as lasting only a little while, after which God will perfect, establish, strengthen, and settle them.

Humility is commanded of all: they are to clothe themselves with it and subject themselves to one another, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Believers are told to humble themselves under God's mighty hand so that he may exalt them in due time.

This document is Paul's Letter to the Ephesians, six chapters written by Paul, an apostle and prisoner of Christ Jesus, to the saints at Ephesus. It moves from what God has done in Christ to how believers should live, ending with spiritual warfare and a personal close. Chapter 1 greets the readers and blesses God for choosing believers before the world's foundation, predestining them for adoption, redeeming them through Christ's blood, and sealing them with the Holy Spirit. Paul prays that they receive wisdom and revelation, and describes the power that raised Christ, seated him at God's right hand, and made him head over all things for the assembly, his body. Chapter 2 says God, rich in mercy, made the readers alive with Christ when they were dead in sins. They are saved by grace through faith, not works, and created for good works. Gentiles, once alienated from Israel, are brought near by Christ's blood. Christ is their peace, breaking down the dividing wall and making one new man of two. They become fellow citizens, God's household, and a holy temple built on Christ as chief cornerstone. Chapter 3 has Paul explain the mystery of Christ, revealed to him: Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the body, and partakers of the promise. He is a servant of the Good News, making God's manifold wisdom known through the assembly. He prays that Christ dwell in their hearts, that they know his love and be filled with God's fullness, and closes with a doxology. Chapter 4 turns practical. Paul urges unity in one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers to equip the saints and build up the body. Readers should put off the old man and put on the new, speak truth, avoid corrupt speech, not grieve the Holy Spirit, and forgive as God forgave them. Chapter 5 calls them to imitate God and walk in love, avoid immorality and covetousness, live as light, be filled with the Spirit, and follow household instructions for wives and husbands, linking marriage to Christ and the assembly. Chapter 6 continues with instructions for children, fathers, servants, and masters, then urges readers to put on the whole armor of God against the devil and spiritual forces, and to pray for all the saints. Paul asks for prayer to speak boldly as an ambassador in chains, announces that Tychicus is being sent to report and comfort them, and ends with blessings of peace, love, faith, and grace.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Paul is the author of a letter to the saints at Ephesus, presenting himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will. Most important is his identity and mission: a prisoner of Christ on behalf of the Gentiles, a servant of the Good News by God's grace, and the very least of all saints, to whom the mystery of Christ was revealed and who was given grace to preach to the Gentiles. The records unfold across chapters. In chapter 1 he greets the Ephesians, gives thanks, and prays for their wisdom, revelation and enlightened hearts. In chapter 3 he describes his calling and troubles, asks them not to lose heart, and bows his knees to the Father for them. In chapter 4, as prisoner in the Lord, he urges them to walk worthily and put off the old life for love and truth. In chapter 6 he calls them to put on God's armor, asks prayer for boldness as an ambassador in chains, sends Tychicus to comfort them, and closes with peace and grace.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: God is presented throughout Paul's Letter to the Ephesians as the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ and the Father of all, over all, through all and in all. He works according to the counsel of his will, is rich in mercy, and loves believers with great love. Chapter 1 shows him blessing believers with every spiritual blessing in Christ, choosing them before the world's foundation, predestining them for adoption, sealing them with the Holy Spirit, and raising Christ from the dead by his mighty power. Chapter 2 describes him making the spiritually dead alive with Christ, giving salvation as a gift, preparing good works, reconciling two groups, and dwelling in the building being built together. Chapter 3 reveals him as creator of all things through Jesus Christ, the one who gave Paul grace, disclosed the long-hidden mystery, and made his manifold wisdom known through the assembly according to his eternal purpose accomplished in Christ. He is the Father from whom every family is named and is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all we ask or think. Chapter 4 calls him the one God and Father, in whose likeness the new man is created and who forgave readers in Christ. Chapter 5 urges imitating him as beloved children, notes his wrath on the disobedient, and speaks of his Kingdom shared with Christ. Chapter 6 closes with his will, his armor, his word as the sword of the Spirit, and him as a source of peace, love and faith.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Jesus Christ, as presented across the six chapters of Paul's Letter to the Ephesians, is the exalted Lord and head of the assembly (the church), his body. The records open with his supremacy: God raised him from the dead, seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, set him far above every rule, authority, power and dominion, put all things under his feet, and made him head over all things for the assembly. In him believers are chosen, redeemed through his blood, forgiven, and given an inheritance, and all things are to be summed up in him. Next comes his reconciling work: he is our peace, makes Jews and Gentiles one, breaks down the dividing wall, abolishes the law of commandments in his flesh, and reconciles both to God through the cross, giving both access to the Father in one Spirit. He is the chief cornerstone of the foundation of the apostles and prophets. Through him God created all things and accomplished his eternal purpose; Paul prays that he may dwell in hearts and that readers may know his love. He then ascends far above the heavens, fills all things, and gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers as gifts, while the body grows into him as head. Finally he is the model of love: he loved the assembly and gave himself up as an offering and sacrifice to God, as savior of the body, sanctifying her by the washing of water with the word to present her holy and without defect. The letter closes by calling him Lord, whom servants serve, and a source with God the Father of peace, love and faith, with grace for all who love him.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God and the one Spirit of the one body; he is the pledge of believers' inheritance and seals them for the day of redemption, so they must not grieve him.

l: saints, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The saints at Ephesus, faithful in Christ Jesus, are greeted with grace and peace by Paul. He notes their faith in the Lord Jesus and love for all saints; after hearing the word of truth and believing, they were sealed with the Holy Spirit.

l: the readers (believers addressed), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The readers are believers addressed in Paul's Letter to the Ephesians. In Chapter 1 they are blessed, chosen to be holy, and given redemption, forgiveness and an inheritance in Christ, existing for the praise of God's glory, with the Holy Spirit as pledge. In Chapter 4 they are called to one hope and members of one body, urged to walk worthily, grow to maturity, put away the old man, put on the new man, and replace falsehood and malice with truth, kindness and forgiveness.

l: the church (body of Christ), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The church is the body of Christ, one body with one Spirit, filled by him who fills all in all. Christ is its head and savior, and it is subject to him. Its members are built up through service until they attain unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God, growing in love as each joint supplies. Christ loved it, gave himself up, cleansed and sanctified it, nourishes and cherishes it, and will present it to himself glorious, holy, without spot, wrinkle or defect.

l: predestination and adoption, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: has_purpose adoption as children through Jesus Christ [according to the good pleasure of God's desire] God predestined believers for adoption as children through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his desire. This is linked to his choosing them before the foundation of the world and is said to be to the praise of the glory of his grace.

l: Christ's resurrection and exaltation, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: is_worked_by God [raised Christ from the dead and seated him in the heavenly places] God worked his mighty strength in Christ by raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand in the heavenly places. This places him far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name, in this age and the one to come, with all things in subjection under his feet.

l: spiritual authorities (powers over which Christ rules), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: located_in heavenly places [opponents in believers' wrestling] The spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places are named alongside the principalities, powers, and world's rulers of the darkness of this age. They are the true opponents of believers, whose wrestling is not against flesh and blood.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Grace is God's gift by which believers are saved through faith, not works, and is linked to the exceeding riches of his kindness in Christ Jesus. In chapter 2 it saves believers; in chapter 3 it is given to Paul, the least of saints, as an administration to the Gentiles to preach Christ's unsearchable riches.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The Gentiles, called "uncircumcision," are a people whose standing changes across the records. Chapter 2 describes them as once separate from Christ, alienated from Israel, strangers to the covenants, without hope and without God, but now made near by Christ's blood, fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household. Chapter 3 declares them fellow heirs, members of the body and partakers of the promise through the Good News; Paul, a prisoner for them, preaches Christ's unsearchable riches to them. Chapter 4 contrasts this by describing their walk in futility, darkened understanding, hardened hearts, and lust, and readers are told not to walk as they do.

l: salvation through faith, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Salvation through faith is believers being saved by grace, a gift of God rather than their own doing or works, which excludes boasting.

l: peace, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: is_preached_to Gentiles [to those far off and those near] Peace is identified with Christ himself, who made both groups one and broke down the dividing wall. He abolished the hostility and the law of commandments in ordinances to make peace, and he preached peace to those far off and those near.

l: holy temple, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The holy temple is the whole building, fitted together and growing in the Lord. It rests on the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus as chief cornerstone, and becomes God's habitation in the Spirit.

l: mystery of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The mystery of Christ, hidden in God for ages and unknown to earlier generations, was made known to Paul by revelation. It is now revealed in the Spirit to God's holy apostles and prophets. Its content: Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the body, and partakers of the promise.

l: assembly, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The assembly is the means by which God's manifold wisdom is now made known to principalities and powers in the heavenly places; the passage ends by giving God glory in it and in Christ Jesus to all generations.

l: Paul's prayer for the readers, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Paul bows before the Father and prays for the readers: that they be strengthened with power through the Spirit in the inner person, that Christ dwell in their hearts through faith, rooted in love, that they grasp Christ's surpassing love with all the saints, and finally be filled with all the fullness of God.

l: the devil, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: uses wiles [armor of God enables standing against them] The devil is described as using wiles against which believers must stand. The armor of God is put on so they can stand against these wiles.

l: church leaders (apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers), Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: has_purpose perfecting the saints [work of serving, building up the body of Christ] Christ gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some shepherds and teachers. Their purpose is the perfecting of the saints, the work of serving, and the building up of the body of Christ.

l: unity of the Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: is_kept_in bond of peace The readers are urged to be eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. It rests on the one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all.

l: old man, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: has_state corrupt [after the lusts of deceit] The old man is the former way of life, which grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit. The readers are told to put it away.

l: new man, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: is_created_in righteousness and holiness of truth [in the likeness of God] The new man is to be put on by the readers as they are renewed in the spirit of their mind. He has been created in the likeness of God in righteousness and holiness of truth.

l: husbands, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Husbands, as addressed in Chapter 5, are commanded to love their wives as Christ loved the assembly and gave himself for her, and as their own bodies. The husband is head of the wife, and loving her is loving himself.

l: wives, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Wives are instructed to be subject to their own husbands as to the Lord in everything, mirroring the assembly's subjection to Christ, and to respect them; the union is tied to the one-flesh passage and Christ-assembly mystery.

l: sexual immorality and uncleanness, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Sexual immorality and uncleanness, with covetousness, are forbidden even to be mentioned among the saints, alongside filthiness and foolish talk. Those who practice them have no inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God; God's wrath falls on the disobedient, so readers must not partner with them.

l: light and darkness, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: A topic contrasting darkness and light for believers: once darkness, now light in the Lord, they walk as children of light bearing goodness, righteousness and truth. They avoid and reprove darkness's secret, shameful deeds; light reveals everything, and Christ will shine on those who awake.

l: Tychicus, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Tychicus is a beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, whom Paul sends to the readers to report on Paul's affairs and state and to comfort their hearts.

l: children, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Children are instructed to obey parents in the Lord because it is right, and to honor father and mother, the first commandment with a promise: well-being and long life on earth.

l: parents, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: nurture_children_in discipline and instruction of the Lord [fathers are told not to provoke children to wrath] Parents are to be obeyed and honored by their children. Fathers are told not to provoke their children to wrath but to nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

l: servants, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Servants are instructed in Chapter 6 to obey earthly masters sincerely, with fear and trembling, as to Christ, serving from the heart rather than when watched, and the Lord Jesus Christ will repay their good, bound or free.

l: masters, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: Masters are commanded to treat servants in kind, give up threatening, and remember they answer to the same impartial Lord Jesus Christ in heaven, who is Master over both servants and masters.

l: armor of God, Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians
s: The armor of God is a set of protective gear believers must put on whole to withstand the evil day and stand. It comprises the belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, gospel-peace footwear, shield of faith quenching fiery darts, helmet of salvation, and sword of the Spirit.

This document is a four-chapter letter from Paul, writing with Timothy, to the saints, overseers and servants at Philippi. It is pastoral and affectionate, combining thanks, personal news and exhortation, and its recurring themes are joy, unity, humility and steadfast faith in Christ despite suffering. Chapter 1 opens with thanks for the Philippians' partnership in the Good News and a prayer that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment. Paul explains that his imprisonment has advanced the gospel, reaching the palace guard and emboldening other brothers, and he rejoices that Christ is proclaimed even by those motivated by envy. He is torn between dying to be with Christ and remaining for their sake, expects to remain, and urges them to stand firm and not fear adversaries. Chapter 2 calls them to unity and humility, using Christ as the model: he emptied himself, took a servant's form, died on the cross, and was exalted by God as Lord. Paul tells them to work out their salvation and shine as lights, and says he is glad even if poured out as a sacrifice. He hopes to send Timothy and is sending Epaphroditus, who nearly died for Christ's work, asking that he be received with honor. Chapter 3 warns against the dogs, evil workers and false circumcision. Paul lists his own credentials, including his Pharisee background and blamelessness under the law, but counts them a loss for Christ. He wants to know Christ, share his sufferings and attain the resurrection, pressing on toward the prize and asking them to imitate him. He contrasts enemies of the cross, whose end is destruction, with believers whose citizenship is in heaven. Chapter 4 urges them to stand firm and asks Euodia and Syntyche to agree. Paul commands rejoicing, gentleness, prayer instead of anxiety, and thinking on what is true and lovely, promising God's peace. He thanks them for their gift, brought through Epaphroditus, says he has learned contentment and can do all things through Christ, promises that God will supply every need, and closes with greetings, including from Caesar's household, and a blessing of grace.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Paul is a servant of Jesus Christ who writes, together with Timothy, to the beloved saints at Philippi, whom he holds in his heart and longs after. Appointed for the defense of the Good News, he is imprisoned yet sees his bonds advancing it. The records open with thanks and prayer that the Philippians' love abound, and he is torn between departing to be with Christ and remaining for their progress. He then urges unity and humility, hopes to send Timothy soon and come himself, and sends Epaphroditus back. Midway he lists his fleshly credentials: circumcised on the eighth day, of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, a persecutor of the church, and blameless under the law. He counts all of it loss for knowing Christ, trusting in righteousness from God through faith rather than his own. He has not yet attained, but presses on toward the goal and offers himself as an example. He closes by exhorting Euodia and Syntyche, urging rejoicing and freedom from anxiety, and affirming that he has learned contentment and receives strength from Christ. He thanks the Philippians for their gift, seeking the fruit to their account.

l: Timothy, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Timothy is a servant of Jesus Christ and co-sender with Paul. Paul hopes to send him soon to the Philippians, since no one else is so like-minded and truly cares for them. He proved himself, serving Paul like a child serving a father.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Jesus Christ is presented as Lord and Savior, the one in whom Paul and the Philippians place their faith, suffering, and hope. Existing in the form of God, he did not grasp at equality but emptied himself, took a servant's form, was made in human likeness, and humbled himself to death on the cross. God then highly exalted him, giving him the name above every name, so that every tongue confesses him Lord. Paul counts all things loss to gain him, to know the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, and says Christ will be magnified in his body by life or death. Christ strengthens Paul to do all things and gives peace and riches. As Savior awaited from heaven, he will change the body of humiliation to conform to his glorious body, by the power through which he subjects all things to himself.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: God appears in Philippians as the Father of Jesus Christ and the God of peace. He began a good work in the Philippian believers and will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ. He works in them to will and to work for his good pleasure. In Chapter 2 he highly exalts Jesus, giving him the name above every name so that every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord to God's glory, and he shows mercy by sparing Epaphroditus from death. Chapter 3 presents him as the source of righteousness by faith and as the one who issued the high calling in Christ Jesus, worshiped in the Spirit. Chapter 4 closes with him as the source of peace surpassing understanding, supplying every need of the Philippians according to his riches in glory, receiving their gift as an acceptable sacrifice, and being given glory forever.

l: Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Philippians is a group of believers, the saints in Jesus Christ at Philippi, together with their overseers and servants. Their defining trait is partnership with Paul, the letter's author, in the Good News from the first day until now. They share in his grace, bonds, and defense of the Good News, and they were the only assembly to share with him in giving and receiving, sending support more than once to his need in Thessalonica. They have always obeyed him, and they have been granted both belief in Christ and suffering for him. The records unfold in four stages. First come greetings, thanks, and a call to stand firm and live worthily. Next comes an exhortation to humility, unity, and shining as lights among a crooked and perverse generation, with praise for their obedience and a request to welcome Epaphroditus. Then they are told to rejoice, beware of false teachers, and imitate Paul, since their citizenship is in heaven. The letter ends by urging steadfastness, prayer over anxiety, and praising their support of Paul.

l: Good News, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: The Good News is furthered by the Philippians' partnership, and Paul's circumstances have turned out to its progress. Paul is appointed for its defense, and some preach Christ from envy and some from good will, yet Christ is proclaimed either way. The Philippians are told to let their way of life be worthy of it and to strive together for its faith.

l: Paul's imprisonment, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Paul's imprisonment, evident to the palace guard as being in Christ, advances the Good News: most brothers grow bold to speak God's word fearlessly, though some preach from selfish ambition to afflict him. Paul trusts it will turn out to his salvation.

l: life and death, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: is_for_paul Christ is life, death is gain Paul says that to him to live is Christ and to die is gain, and that Christ will be magnified in his body whether by life or by death. He is hard pressed between the two, since departing to be with Christ is far better but remaining in the flesh brings fruit and is more needful for the Philippians. He concludes that he will remain for their progress and joy in the faith.

l: Epaphroditus, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Epaphroditus is Paul's brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier, and the Philippians' apostle and servant of Paul's need. He risked his life for Christ's work, supplying what they lacked in serving Paul. He fell nearly fatally ill, but God showed mercy. Longing for the Philippians, he was troubled that they had heard. Paul sends him back, asking them to receive and honor him joyfully.

l: humility and unity, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
