s: Paul calls for being of one mind, one accord, and the same love, doing nothing from rivalry or conceit but counting others better than oneself and looking to others' interests. Christ's example is held up as the pattern, and the believers are further told to act without complaining and arguing.

l: Christ's self-emptying and exaltation, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: The text describes Christ emptying himself, taking a servant's form, being found in human form, and becoming obedient to death on a cross. This is followed by God's exaltation of him, giving him the name above every name, with universal bowing in heaven, on earth, and under the earth and confession that Jesus Christ is Lord.

l: enemies of the cross of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Many whom Paul, weeping, calls enemies of the cross of Christ: their god is the belly, glory in shame, minds on earthly things, and their end is destruction.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: The law is the standard under which Paul was a Pharisee and was found blameless in the righteousness which is in the law. He counts that righteousness as not his own basis for standing, preferring the righteousness through faith in Christ.

l: righteousness, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Paul distinguishes the righteousness of the law, which he once had and found blameless, from the righteousness which is from God by faith in Christ. He wants to be found in Christ not having a righteousness of his own, but the one from God through faith.

l: resurrection, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Paul wants to know the power of Christ's resurrection and hopes by any means to attain the resurrection from the dead. He also expects Christ to change the body of humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory.

l: the goal and prize of the high calling, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: Paul presses on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. He says he has not yet taken hold of it, but forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what is ahead.

l: Euodia, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: labored_with Paul (author) [in the Good News] Euodia is exhorted by name to think the same way in the Lord. She is among the women who labored with Paul in the Good News.

l: Syntyche, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: labored_with Paul (author) [in the Good News] Syntyche is exhorted by name to think the same way in the Lord. She is among the women who labored with Paul in the Good News.

l: gift from the Philippians, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: The Philippians' gift, carried by Epaphroditus and received by Paul, is called a sweet-smelling, well-pleasing sacrifice to God; Paul stresses he seeks the fruit credited to their account, recalling earlier aid sent to Thessalonica.

l: rejoicing, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: is_commanded always in the Lord [Paul's exhortation to the Philippians] Paul commands the readers to rejoice in the Lord always and repeats the command. He himself rejoices greatly in the Lord that the Philippians have revived their thought for him.

l: contentment, Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
s: is_learned_by Paul (author) [in being filled or hungry, abounding or in need] Paul says he has learned to be content in whatever state he is in, knowing how to be humbled and how to abound, to be filled and to be hungry. He ties this ability to Christ who strengthens him, and says he does not speak out of lack.

This document is a letter from Paul and Timothy to the saints and faithful brothers at Colossae, presented in four chapters. It centers on Christ's supremacy and what that means for how the Colossians live. Chapter 1 opens with thanksgiving for their faith, love, and hope, learned from Epaphras, and a prayer that they be filled with the knowledge of God's will and bear fruit. It portrays the Son as the image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation, creator of all things, head of the assembly, and reconciler through the blood of his cross. Paul rejoices in his sufferings and proclaims the once-hidden mystery, Christ in you, the hope of glory. Chapter 2 describes Paul's struggle for the Colossians, the Laodiceans, and others who have not seen him, so they may know Christ, in whom all wisdom is hidden. He warns against philosophy, empty deceit, and human tradition, stating that the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily in Christ, who forgave trespasses, nailed the handwriting of ordinances to the cross, and triumphed over principalities and powers. Hence no one should judge them over food, feast days, Sabbaths, or angel worship, and rules like 'Don't handle, nor taste, nor touch' are questioned. Chapter 3 turns practical: having been raised with Christ, readers should set their minds on things above, put to death vices, put off the old man and put on the new, and clothe themselves in compassion, kindness, humility, forgiveness, and love. It gives instructions to wives, husbands, children, fathers, and servants. Chapter 4 closes with directions to masters, a call to persevere in prayer, and wise speech toward outsiders. Tychicus and Onesimus are sent to report and comfort, greetings come from Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras, Luke, and Demas, the Laodiceans are to be greeted and letters exchanged, Archippus is told to fulfill his ministry, and Paul signs in his own hand, asking them to remember his chains.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Paul is an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will, and a servant of the Good News and of the assembly, entrusted with a stewardship from God. Writing with Timothy to the saints at Colossae, he gives thanks and prays for them. He rejoices in his sufferings for their sake and labors, striving by Christ's working in him, to present everyone perfect in Christ. He struggles for the Colossians and those at Laodicea, and though absent in the flesh he is with them in spirit, warning them against deceptive philosophy and human rules. By the end he is imprisoned for the mystery of Christ, alongside fellow prisoner Aristarchus and fellow worker Justus. He asks for prayer that God open a door for the word, sends Tychicus and Onesimus, relays greetings, directs that the letter be shared with the Laodiceans, and closes in his own hand, asking them to remember his chains.

l: Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Christ, called Jesus Christ and the Son of God's love, is presented as supreme over creation and the church. Chapter 1 describes him as the image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation and from the dead, through whom and for whom all things were created and are held together. He is head of the assembly, and through his cross's blood he redeems and reconciles all things. Chapter 2 stresses that all the fullness of the Deity dwells in him bodily and all wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him. He is head of principalities and powers, over which he triumphed, and the body grows from him as Head. Readers are to walk in him and be made full in him. Chapter 3 places him seated at God's right hand as the readers' life, to be revealed in glory with them. He forgave them, modeling how they should forgive one another, and he is all and in all, erasing distinctions among people. They are to do everything in his name and serve him as Lord.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: God is presented as the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ. In the first chapter he makes believers fit for the saints' inheritance in light, delivers them from darkness into his Son's Kingdom, and makes known the mystery's glory among the Gentiles. Next, he raised Christ from the dead, makes believers alive with him, forgives trespasses, and causes the body to grow. Finally, Christ sits at his right hand, his wrath falls on the disobedient, he chooses believers as holy and beloved, his peace rules hearts, and he shows no partiality.

l: recipients of the letter (Colossians), Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: The recipients are the believers at Colossae, described as saints and faithful brothers in Christ who learned the grace of God in truth from Epaphras. They are praised for faith in Christ Jesus, love toward all the saints, and hope laid up in the heavens. Once alienated and enemies in mind through evil deeds, they have been delivered into the Kingdom of the Son and reconciled through Christ's death, with forgiveness of sins, to be presented holy and blameless if they remain grounded and steadfast. Paul prays they be filled with knowledge of God's will, walk worthily, and bear fruit. They are urged to walk in Christ, rooted and established, and warned against philosophy, observances, angel worship, and ordinances, since they were circumcised, buried and raised with Christ, made alive, and died to the elemental spirits of the world. Having been raised with Christ, their life is hidden with him in God. They are to seek things above, put to death earthly vices, put off the old man, put on the new man and its virtues, and walk in love, thankfulness, and teaching. Finally, they receive instructions on prayer, wise conduct toward outsiders, greetings, reading the letter from Laodicea, and Archippus's ministry.

l: Epaphras, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Epaphras is a faithful, beloved servant of Christ and one of the Colossians' own. He sends greetings, prays constantly that they stand perfect and complete in God's will, and, as Paul testifies, has great zeal for them and for those in Laodicea and Hierapolis.

l: Good News, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: The Good News carries the word of truth and hope laid up in heaven. It reached the Colossians, bears fruit and grows in them and worldwide, was proclaimed in all creation under heaven, and Paul became its servant.

l: mystery of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: The mystery was hidden for ages and generations, then revealed to God's saints; its glorious riches are made known among the Gentiles as Christ in you, the hope of glory, whom Paul and companions proclaim, teaching everyone in wisdom.

l: redemption and reconciliation, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: has_purpose present believers holy, without defect and blameless In the Son believers have redemption, the forgiveness of sins, and have been delivered from the power of darkness into his Kingdom. Through him God reconciles all things to himself, whether on earth or in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross. The Colossians, once alienated, have been reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to be presented holy and blameless.

l: creation, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: includes thrones, dominions, principalities, powers [visible and invisible things] All things in the heavens and on the earth, visible and invisible, including thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, were created by, through and for the Son. He is before all things and in him all things are held together. The Son is called firstborn of all creation, and the Good News has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven.

l: principalities and powers, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Christ is the head of all principality and power. In this unit they are stripped by Christ, who made an open show of them and triumphed over them in the cross.

l: false teachers (anyone who robs you), Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: attempts_to_rob the Colossian recipients (you) [through philosophy and vain deceit] These unnamed people are warned against as ones who might delude the recipients with persuasive speech, rob them through philosophy and vain deceit, judge them over food and festivals, or rob them of their prize. One such person is described as dwelling in things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, and not holding firmly to the Head.

l: handwriting in ordinances, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: A handwriting in ordinances stood against the Colossian recipients, but God wiped it out, removing it by nailing it to the cross.

l: philosophy and tradition of men, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: is_not_according_to Christ Jesus the Lord [follows elemental spirits of the world] Philosophy and vain deceit, according to the tradition of men and the elemental spirits of the world and not according to Christ, are what the recipients must guard against being robbed by. The precepts and doctrines of men are said to appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body, but to have no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

l: dietary and festival observances, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: is_a shadow of the things to come Eating, drinking, feast days, new moons, and Sabbath days are things for which the recipients are told to let no one judge them. They are called a shadow of things to come, while the body is Christ's. Rules such as 'Don't handle, nor taste, nor touch' are said to concern things that perish with use.

l: old man, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: The old man is something the readers have put off, along with his doings, which include lying. He is contrasted with the new man.

l: new man, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: is_renewed_after_image_of Creator (God) [in knowledge] The new man is what the readers have put on, and he is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator. In this new state there is no distinction between Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, or free, because Christ is all and in all.

l: vices of earthly nature, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Earthly vices, including sexual immorality, uncleanness, evil desire, and covetousness (idolatry), must be put to death, along with anger, malice, slander and lying; God's wrath comes on the disobedient for them, as readers once walked in them.

l: Christian virtues, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Christian virtues are qualities readers are told to put on: compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, perseverance, with mutual bearing and forgiveness as Christ forgave. Love crowns them as the bond of perfection; peace, thankfulness, and Christ's word are commended.

l: wives, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: are_commanded_to be in subjection to husbands [as is fitting in the Lord] Wives are told to be in subjection to their husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

l: husbands, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: are_commanded_to love wives [not be bitter against them] Husbands are told to love their wives and not be bitter against them.

l: children, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: are_commanded_to obey parents [in all things] Children are told to obey their parents in all things, because this pleases the Lord.

l: fathers, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: are_commanded_not_to provoke children [so they won't be discouraged] Fathers are told not to provoke their children, so that the children won't be discouraged.

l: servants, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: are_commanded_to obey masters [in all things, with sincerity, fearing God] Servants are told to obey their masters according to the flesh in all things, not just when watched, but in singleness of heart, fearing God. They are to work heartily as for the Lord, knowing they will receive the reward of the inheritance from the Lord Christ, whom they serve. The one who does wrong will be repaid, with no partiality.

l: Tychicus, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Tychicus is a beloved brother, faithful servant and fellow bondservant in the Lord, whom Paul sends to the recipients to report all his affairs, learn their circumstances and comfort their hearts.

l: Onesimus, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: Onesimus is a faithful, beloved brother and one of the Colossian letter's recipients, sent with Tychicus to report everything happening where Paul is.

l: this letter, Paul’s Letter to the Colossians
s: A letter written by Paul, ending with companions' greetings and his own handwritten greeting; it is read among its recipients, then in the Laodiceans' assembly, who in turn share their Laodicea letter.

This document is the First Letter to Timothy, a pastoral epistle in six chapters in which Paul, an apostle, instructs Timothy, his true child in the faith, on how to guard sound teaching and order the community at Ephesus. The most important figures are Paul, Timothy, and Christ Jesus, with Hymenaeus and Alexander appearing as cautionary examples. Chapter 1 opens with greetings and Paul's charge that Timothy stay at Ephesus and command certain men not to teach a different doctrine or follow myths and endless genealogies. The goal of the command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. Paul thanks Christ for appointing him despite his past as a blasphemer and persecutor, calling himself the chief of sinners who received mercy. He urges Timothy to wage the good warfare and names Hymenaeus and Alexander, who shipwrecked their faith. Chapter 2 turns to worship: prayers should be made for all people, including kings, because God desires all to be saved and Christ Jesus is the one mediator who gave himself as a ransom for all. Men are told to pray without anger, women to dress modestly, and the author does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man. Chapter 3 lists qualifications for overseers and servants, including blamelessness, self-control, good household management, and testing before service. It describes the assembly as God's house and ends by declaring the mystery of godliness great: God revealed in the flesh and received up in glory. Chapter 4 warns that in later times some will fall away, following doctrines of demons that forbid marriage and certain foods. The writer insists that all creation is good when received with thanksgiving, and urges Timothy to refuse profane fables, train in godliness, be an example despite his youth, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching, and watch himself and his teaching. Chapter 5 gives guidance for treating older and younger men and women, with extended rules on widows, including who should be enrolled and the duty of families to support their own. It also covers honoring elders, requiring two or three witnesses for accusations, avoiding prejudice and hasty laying on of hands, and using a little wine for the stomach. Chapter 6 addresses bondservants, condemns those who teach differently and treat godliness as gain, and says godliness with contentment is great gain while love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Timothy is told to flee these things, pursue righteousness, fight the good fight, and keep the commandment until Christ appears. Rich people are charged to hope in God and share, and Timothy is told to guard what was entrusted to him and avoid empty chatter.

Paul is an apostle of Jesus Christ by God's commandment, writing to Timothy, his true child in faith. Once a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent man, he obtained mercy because he acted ignorantly in unbelief. Calling himself chief of sinners, he was counted faithful, appointed to service, and entrusted with the Good News; he delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan.

Timothy is a young man, addressed as Paul's true child in faith and called a man of God, who is stationed at Ephesus. Paul charges him to command certain men not to teach a different doctrine, in keeping with earlier prophecies, so that he may wage the good warfare with faith and a good conscience. He has a gift given by prophecy with the laying on of the elders' hands, is nourished in the words of the faith, and suffers frequent infirmities. He is urged not to let anyone despise his youth but to be an example to believers in word, conduct, love, spirit, faith and purity, to devote himself to reading, exhortation and teaching, and to instruct the brothers. Finally he is told to flee the love of money, pursue righteousness and godliness, fight the good fight, take hold of eternal life, keep the commandment blameless, charge the rich, guard what was committed to him, and turn from false knowledge and false teachers.

Christ Jesus is presented in 1 Timothy as both a man and Lord, the hope of Paul and Timothy, and the source of grace, mercy, and peace alongside God. He came into the world to save sinners, enabling and appointing Paul and showing patience as an example for believers. He is the only mediator between God and men, who gave himself as a ransom for all. He made the good confession before Pontius Pilate. His appearing is awaited at the right time, when he will be shown as the blessed and only Ruler, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light.

God, as portrayed across the six chapters of 1 Timothy, is the one and only God: Savior and Father, blessed, living, and the eternal, immortal, invisible King who alone is wise and alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light. The chapters open with praise of him and with his commandment as the basis of Paul's apostleship. They then stress his desire that all people be saved and come to know the truth, and that prayer for all is good and acceptable to him. He is called the living God, whose house is the assembly, and the closing statement says he was revealed in the flesh and received up in glory. He created foods and every creature as good, to be received with thanksgiving and sanctified by his word. He is Savior of all men, especially believers. He accepts care for family, and the true widow hopes in him. He gives life to all things and richly provides everything to enjoy, so the rich are told to hope in him rather than in riches.
Hymenaeus is a man named in 1 Timothy 1 who rejected faith and a good conscience, shipwrecking his faith; Paul consequently delivered him to Satan to learn not to blaspheme.

was_delivered_to Satan [by Paul, to learn not to blaspheme] Alexander is named alongside Hymenaeus as having made shipwreck concerning the faith. Paul delivered him to Satan that he might be taught not to blaspheme.

The false teachers at Ephesus are men who teach a different doctrine, devoting themselves to myths, endless genealogies, and disputes. Having missed the mark, they turn to vain talking and want to be law teachers without understanding what they affirm. Later they are described as conceited, knowing nothing, obsessed with word battles that breed envy, strife, insults, and evil suspicions, and they treat godliness as a means of gain. Timothy is told to command them to stop and to withdraw from them; some have wandered from the faith.

The law is good when used lawfully. It is intended not for the righteous but for the lawless, ungodly, and sinners, such as murderers, liars, and the sexually immoral, and anything contrary to sound doctrine and the Good News.

is_according_to godliness [words of the Lord Jesus Christ] Sound doctrine is described as the words of the Lord Jesus Christ and the doctrine according to godliness. Misbehavior by bondservants risks causing it to be blasphemed, and those who do not consent to it are labeled conceited teachers of a different doctrine. Timothy is told to teach and exhort these things and to guard what was committed to him.
Adam, formed first before Eve and not deceived, is cited as grounds for restricting women's teaching.
Eve, a woman formed after Adam, is described in Chapter 2 as having been deceived and consequently falling into disobedience.

are_desired_to pray [in every place, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting] Men are included among all people for whom prayer is to be made, and God desires their salvation. The author wants men in every place to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting. Christ Jesus is the mediator between God and men.

Women are instructed in Chapter 2 to adorn themselves with decent, modest clothing and good works befitting godliness, to learn quietly in full submission, and are said to be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love, holiness, and sobriety.

Prayer for all people is an exhortation, placed first, to offer petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings for everyone, explicitly including kings and those in high places, so believers may lead a tranquil, quiet life in godliness and reverence, which is good and acceptable to God.

God desires all people to be saved and to come to full knowledge of the truth. Christ Jesus gave himself as a ransom for all. The text also says the woman will be saved through her childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness with sobriety.

excludes braided hair, gold, pearls, expensive clothing [not the manner of adornment] Women are to dress decently with modesty and propriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or expensive clothing. Their adornment is to be good works, appropriate for women professing godliness. They are also to learn in quietness with full submission.

l: women's teaching and authority restriction, 1 Timothy
s: A restriction in Chapter 2 stating the author does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over a man, but to be in quietness; it is grounded in Adam being formed first, then Eve, and in the woman's deception.

The overseer is a role-holder who desires a good work and cares for God's assembly. The records stress strict qualifications: he must be without reproach, husband of one wife, temperate, gentle, and good at teaching, and not greedy. He must rule his household well, keeping obedient children, since failure there would unfit him. He must not be a new convert, lest he fall into the devil's condemnation, and must have good outside testimony.

Servants are a group defined by requirements: reverent, not double-tongued, wine-addicted or greedy for money, holding the faith's mystery in a pure conscience, husbands of one wife, ruling households well. They are tested first and serve only if blameless; their wives must also be worthy. Those who serve well gain good standing and boldness in faith.

God's assembly is God's house, the assembly of the living God and the pillar and ground of the truth. The writer gives instructions on proper conduct within it, and the overseer is charged with caring for it, his fitness shown by ruling his own house.

The mystery of godliness is declared, without controversy, to be great; it unfolds as God revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached, believed on, and received up in glory.
The Spirit speaks expressly, warning that in later times some will fall away from the faith. This is the source of the prophetic warning that opens the chapter.

l: those who fall away from the faith, 1 Timothy
s: In later times some will fall away, heeding seducing spirits and doctrines of demons. Hypocritical liars, their consciences branded as with a hot iron, lead them, forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods.
Foods are good creatures of God, made to be received with thanksgiving by believers; nothing is rejected when received thus, being sanctified through God's word and prayer.

Believers are those who know the truth and receive God's creation with thanksgiving. The addressee is told to be an example to them in word, way of life, love, spirit, faith, and purity. God is the Savior of all men, especially of them.

Godliness with contentment is a teaching presented across two chapters. Chapter 4 urges exercising oneself toward godliness, which outweighs bodily exercise, holding value in all things and promise for life now and to come. Chapter 6 calls it great gain, unlike treating godliness as profit, with contentment shown as satisfaction with food and clothing.

The addressee is told to command and teach these things and to attend to teaching until the writer comes. He is to pay attention to his teaching and continue in it, for doing so will save both himself and his hearers. The good doctrine is also what has nourished him.

True widows are to be honored: desolate, hoping in God, and continuing in petitions and prayers night and day. Enrollment requires being at least sixty, wife of one man, and approved for good works such as raising children and hospitality. Families relieve their own widows first; then the assembly relieves the rest.

Younger widows are a group the text says should be refused enrollment as widows. It warns they may grow wanton against Christ, learn idleness, gossip and meddle from house to house, and some have already turned to Satan. It advises they marry, bear children, and rule households.

Elders are a group in Chapter 5 who deserve double honor when they rule well, especially those laboring in word and teaching, supported by ox and wages sayings. Accusations against them need two or three witnesses, and those who sin are reproved publicly to instill fear.

has_duty_to show piety to family and repay parents [to learn first; acceptable to God] Children and grandchildren of a widow are told to learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents. This is described as acceptable in the sight of God.
